claims.statement: FDA granted accelerated approval to elamipretide (brand name FORZINITY) to improve muscle strength in adult and pediatric patients with Barth syndrome weighing at least 30 kg; this is the first FDA-approved therapy for Barth syndrome.

context.population: adult and pediatric patients with Barth syndrome weighing at least 30 kg

extractedEvidence.quote: FORZINITY is indicated to improve muscle strength in adult and pediatric patients with Barth syndrome weighing at least 30 kg.
September 19, 2025

claims.statement: The Barth syndrome indication was granted under accelerated approval, based on an intermediate clinical endpoint (knee extensor muscle strength) rather than a demonstrated clinical-benefit endpoint; FDA required a confirmatory randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in patients 5 years and older to verify and describe clinical benefit, with the confirmatory study enrolling March 2026-March 2028 and final reporting due by March 2030. Continued approval is contingent on that verification.

context.population: Barth syndrome patients, confirmatory trial cohort age 5+

extractedEvidence.quote: It is approved under accelerated approval pursuant to section 506(c)
Conduct a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in patients 5 years and older with Barth syndrome to verify and describe the clinical benefit
This indication is approved under accelerated approval based on an improvement in knee extensor muscle strength, an intermediate clinical endpoint.
Continued approval for this indication may be contingent upon verification and description of clinical benefit in a confirmatory trial(s).

reviewFlags: accelerated approval status is conditional; monitor confirmatory trial (targeted completion 2030) for outcome

claims.statement: Elamipretide is a synthetic aromatic-cationic tetrapeptide (a Szeto-Schiller peptide, SS-31) that concentrates in the inner mitochondrial membrane and is described as binding cardiolipin to support mitochondrial bioenergetics; its molecular formula is C32H49N9O5.

extractedEvidence.quote: C32H49N9O5

reviewFlags: cardiolipin-binding mechanism claim sourced from general compound literature, not verbatim-quoted from a fetched primary mechanistic source this session; confirm with a dedicated pharmacology review at next pass

claims.statement: The FORZINITY label specifies a recommended dose of 40 mg subcutaneously once daily for patients weighing at least 30 kg, with a reduced dose of 20 mg daily for adults with severe renal impairment (eGFR <30 mL/min) not on dialysis; injections are rotated between the abdomen (at least 2 inches from the navel) and outer thigh.

context.population: Barth syndrome patients weighing at least 30 kg (label population)
context.useCase: labeled dosing for approved Barth syndrome indication - trial/label protocol context only, not a use recommendation for any other population
context.doseText: 40 mg subcutaneously once daily (20 mg daily if severe renal impairment, eGFR <30 mL/min, not on dialysis) - label text, not a use recommendation

Store refrigerated at 2°C to 8°C (36°F to 46°F). Do not freeze.
Discard vials 8 days after first opening.

reviewFlags: must not be generalized beyond the labeled Barth syndrome population or beyond the FORZINITY product

claims.statement: The most common adverse reactions reported for FORZINITY are injection site reactions (erythema, pain, induration, pruritus, bruising, and urticaria); the label also notes eosinophilia that typically resolved within 6-12 months, a hypersensitivity warning requiring monitoring for allergic reactions including rash and respiratory symptoms with possible need for epinephrine, and that the product is not approved for use in neonates due to benzyl alcohol content (20 mg/mL).

extractedEvidence.quote: Most common adverse reactions are injection site reactions
Serious hypersensitivity to elamipretide or any of the excipients in FORZINITY.
Not approved for use in neonates

reviewFlags: adverse-event profile derives from the labeled Barth syndrome population under supervised dosing; not established for unsupervised gray-market subcutaneous use at other doses

claims.statement: In MMPOWER-3, the phase 3 randomized controlled trial of elamipretide in primary mitochondrial myopathy (a different, non-approved indication from Barth syndrome), elamipretide did not meet its co-primary endpoints - change in 6-minute walk test distance and change in Primary Mitochondrial Myopathy Symptom Assessment (PMMSA) total fatigue score - versus placebo, despite an earlier phase 2 trial having shown improvement on patient-reported outcomes without benefit on the 6-minute walk test. The treatment was reported tolerable, with mostly mild-to-moderate adverse events.

context.population: adults with genetically confirmed primary mitochondrial myopathy
context.useCase: primary mitochondrial myopathy - efficacy trial, NOT an FDA-approved indication

claims.statement: Gray-market vendors marketing elamipretide under the research name SS-31 (unrelated to the FDA-approved FORZINITY product and its Barth syndrome indication) promote it for anti-aging, cellular energy/ATP production, endurance, exercise recovery, and fatigue resistance in general consumers; these use cases are not supported by any approved indication or by the published controlled human trial evidence identified this session, which involved a different investigational program (primary mitochondrial myopathy) that failed its primary endpoints. The reviewed vendor page does disclose that SS-31/elamipretide is investigational and 'not approved to diagnose, treat, cure, or prevent any disease,' but this disclosure follows extensive benefit-oriented marketing language.

context.population: general consumers of gray-market/research-labeled peptide products
context.useCase: anti-aging, energy, endurance, and recovery marketing claims

reviewFlags: misinformation-adjacent: general-population anti-aging/performance marketing claims lack supporting human outcome evidence and fall outside the sole approved indication
do not infer general-population human efficacy from the Barth syndrome accelerated-approval data or from animal/in-vitro mitochondrial mechanism data

conflicts.summary: Elamipretide carries a narrow FDA accelerated approval (Barth syndrome muscle strength, based on an intermediate endpoint with confirmatory trial pending) alongside a documented phase 3 efficacy failure in a separate indication (primary mitochondrial myopathy) and widespread gray-market marketing for unrelated general-wellness/anti-aging uses; these three evidence strands must be kept distinct and not blended into a single 'proven effective' narrative.

reviewReasons: Expansion-batch evidence packet requires human review before publication.
